# Book Two · Chapter 20: Cheaper than deciding
*Lot Fourteen* · Version 1.11 · EN

## Day Two Hundred and Nine · Thursday 30 April

He got in at twenty past eleven and the light in the small room was on.

That is not usual. She works late perhaps twice a week and she does not wait up for anybody. She has never once in seven months been in that room at that hour on a night when there was nothing on the desk.

There was nothing on the desk.

"Come in and shut it," said Annie.

He shut it, which is the second time that door has been shut with him inside the room.

"It is the thirtieth of April," she said.

"Yes."

"You told me on the twentieth of March that it would be finished by the end of April. I made you say it again on the first, because I wanted it to be a date and not a thing a man says at midnight." She had her hands flat on the desk. "It is the thirtieth of April at twenty past eleven. Report."

He stood at the corner of the desk and did it in order and it took four minutes.

The house on the river closed to the public yesterday. Mrs Sunwoo has three more lunches in the diary and does not need any of them.

Nam Byung-hee has two trucks, no chair, no work and no association standing. All five have signed Chairman Woo's paper, seven years, the same document as the anchor cargo. Mr Kwon was the last of them, on the twenty-seventh.

The five halves come onto the market between the middle of May and the middle of June, five separate afternoons, and there is one buyer on that coast with money in her hand and it is not a metaphor.

Mr Ok is a hand and was frightened on Monday and nothing else has happened to him or will. The second copy went into his own filing on the twelfth of March and he can put his hand on it in twenty minutes, which is the only thing this month that has turned out smaller than it looked.

The man who chose her has nine lines of description and a sentence and no name.

"You have left one out."

"I have not left it out. I put it last because it is the only part of the month that is finished, and I did not want it standing in front of the parts that are not."

"Then say it."

"The five are yours."

* * *

Annie put the pen down, which she does not do in the middle of a report.

"Say that so that I can check it."

"Every one of the five was told who asked Chairman Woo, individually, by me, on the day he signed." Georgij did not decorate any of it. "Not by telephone and not through the association. I drove to four yards and a kitchen and I said the same sentence in the same words five times."

"The sentence."

"That a woman on the river wanted a lane out of Ulsan. That Chairman Woo was asked. That he then made his own decision about his own quay with his own money."

"And what did it cost me."

"Nothing." He did not soften it. "Not one won. Not one hour. Not one telephone call, and there is nothing coming later that I have not put in front of you tonight."

* * *

Annie sat with that for a moment.

"On the third of April you stood in this room and told me that in about three weeks five frightened men were going to be extremely grateful to somebody, and that the somebody could be me."

"I did."

"It is the thirtieth."

"Twenty-seven days," said Georgij.

Annie almost smiled at that, and it did not get anywhere near her face, and she did not say the thing that goes there.

"Then there is one more instruction and you are not going to like it," she said.

"Go on."

"Go back and tell all five that they do not owe me anything."

* * *

Georgij did not answer straight away.

"That is the part that is worth having," he said.

"I know what it is worth. I have had gratitude in this business for twenty years and I can price it in about four seconds." Annie had not raised her voice. "A man who thinks he owes you is a man somebody else can collect from. Not me. Somebody. And he will pay, because he has been waiting a year to feel better."

"They will not believe it."

"Then say it twice."

"I will say it once and properly." He did not look away. "I am not driving back down there this week. Five men who have just signed seven years do not want to see me again in April." He said it in the flat voice. "It will keep."

"It will keep," said Annie.

She picked the pen back up, and it was the only thing she let go of that evening without finishing, and neither of them noticed at the time.

* * *

"That is the month," said Georgij.

"That is the month."

Annie did not say anything about any of it, which he had expected, because she does not congratulate people and it has never once occurred to her that anybody might want her to.

"Now the other thing," she said.

"Yes."

"I am not going to ask it gently and I am not going to give you a way of answering it that lets you past. I have thought about how to put it since about six o'clock." She looked at him. "Did you enjoy it."

He did not answer straight away, and she let him not answer.

"Yes," he said. "Once. For about a second and a half, at a gate, at four o'clock this afternoon."

He had promised her that answer on the third of April, and he had brought back the version that cost him something.

"Say what it was."

"She asked what would happen if she talked anyway. And I told her I would come back a fourth time and there would be nothing in my hands then either." He said it perfectly evenly. "It is true, and it was the correct thing to say, and I would say it again in that position tomorrow, and I enjoyed saying it."

Annie sat back.

"And the rest of the month."

"No. Not one minute of it. Kwon's yard, no. The telephone call on the twenty-third, no, and I said I was sorry to a man who did not want it. Mr Ok at his own wall, no. This afternoon, none of it, and I have never wanted less to be anywhere in my life than I did in that office."

"And the one second and a half."

"The one second and a half, yes."

"How do you know?"

"Because she told me." He looked at the edge of the desk. "She said it was the only thing I had said all day that I enjoyed, and she said it in the voice she reads things in." He did not look up. "Then I got on a train and had four hours and could not find an answer I was prepared to write down."

"Then she is better at this than I am."

"She is not. She had the advantage of not caring what the answer was."

Annie thought about that for a moment and let it go, and it was not agreement.

"Say the rest of what you came in here to say," she said. "You have had four hours and you have been standing there working out how to get to it since I said report."

"I would like the ceiling back."

The clock in the hall did the thing it does at the quarter.

"Say it properly," said Annie.

"On the third of April I asked you to take it off me and you did, and it was the right thing to ask for and I would ask again." He had his hands behind his back. "I am asking you to put it back on. The price before it is paid, in this room, every time, and if there is no time to ask then I tell you the same night. I would like it to start tomorrow morning."

"No," said Annie.

He did not move.

"Say why," he said, "because you have got a reason and I would rather have it than the word."

"Because you are not asking me for a ceiling." She said it without any heat at all. "You are asking me to be the thing that stops you, and a man who has somebody to stop him has to decide once, on a Thursday in April, and never again."

"That is not what I am doing."

"It is exactly what you are doing and you know the shape of it better than anybody alive, because it is what you have done to eleven people since October." She did not raise her voice. "You put a rule in front of a man so that he does not have to make the decision again in June. It works every single time, and it works because a rule is cheaper than deciding."

Georgij stood there and did not have anything at all.

"I am not going to be your conscience," said Annie. "Not because I do not want the job. Because I would be extremely good at it and you would never have to do it again. In four years you would be somebody who does whatever is in front of him and comes home and has it audited."

"And if I get it wrong."

"Then you will get it wrong, and you will find out, and it will cost somebody something." She held his eye. "That is what it costs to be the person deciding. You have had two months of it now and I am not going to take it off you because the second month was unpleasant."

He did not say anything for a while.

"You are going to have to do it every time," she said. "Every single time, on the afternoon, in the room, with nobody in it but you. And there will be no version where you get to have decided already."

"That is worse than the ceiling."

"Yes. It is also the only one of the two that is worth anything, and you would have told anybody else exactly that."

He looked at the desk for a moment.

"May I say one thing that is not an argument?"

"Say it."

"I have not been afraid of very much since October," said Georgij. "I have been afraid of four things and I could name all four. As of this afternoon there are five, and the fifth one is that I am going to be all right about it."

He had counted his fears the way he counts everything else, and the new one was about himself.

Annie did not answer that for a moment.

"Yes," she said. "That is the correct one to be afraid of, and I would have been disappointed in you if it had taken you until June."

She got up and came round the desk.

"Sit down on the floor."

He sat down at the side of the desk with his back against it, which is where he sits. She sat on the arm of the reading chair, which is not sitting. Neither of them said anything for a while.

"What happens to her now," said Annie.

She has not asked one question about that woman since the third of April, and he had stopped expecting her to.

"Nothing happens to her. That is the whole of it. Two trucks, no work, and a name that is finished on that coast. Nobody on it will employ her, because employing her is a statement, and nobody makes a statement about a woman who has just been put out by her own six."

"And she is fifty-eight."

"She is fifty-eight, and she is the most competent person I have sat in a room with since December, and I am saying that as a piece of information and not as a sentiment."

Annie looked at the window.

"Then somebody should employ her."

"Yes," said Georgij. "In about four months. Not by me, and she is never going to know where it came from."

"Say the reasons and put them in the order they actually go in."

"Three of them." He set them out. "She is good and she is going to be wasted, and that is the one I would put last if I am being honest about the order. She is honest, and there is going to be very little of that on that coast by June."

"And the first."

"Somebody who has been armed once can be armed again. A woman with nothing is a woman who says yes to the next man who arrives with a page, and I have spent six weeks finding out how cheap that is to arrange."

"That is the one that matters," said Annie.

"That is the one that matters. It closes the last hole in the whole of it."

"And there is a fourth and you have not said it."

"There is a fourth and I would sooner it were not there."

"Say it anyway."

"The man who chose her is going to hear about it." Georgij said it flatly. "He will hear that his instrument was taken apart in six weeks and then picked up off the floor by the same hand, and there is nothing at all he can do with that except sit with it."

"And why four months," said Annie.

"Because in May it is a payment. She would take it, and it would be the last thing that ever happened to her with my hand on it, and I would have bought my way out of this afternoon for the price of a job." He did not move. "She said something to me at a gate today that I have not got an answer to. I am not going to answer it with a favour."

"There is one more thing," she said eventually, "and it is not about any of that."

"Mistress."

"You have not slept properly since the eighteenth of March, and neither has anybody in this house who has been paying attention. That is Mrs Seo and Jang and me, and Mr Ku, who is the only one of the four to have said anything about it."

"He has not said anything about it."

"He said something to you on an expressway on the fourteenth of April about a yard in Gimhae." She was looking at the window and not at him. "He came and told Mrs Seo that he had said it and that he was not sure whether he should have. He has been worrying about it for a fortnight."

Georgij put his head back against the side of the desk.

"Tell him it was the most useful thing anybody said to me all month."

"Tell him yourself. He is on the early rota."

"Yes, Mistress."

She put her hand down without looking away from the window and left it in his hair, and after a while his shoulders came down about an inch, and he had known this time that they were up.

# Book Two · Chapter 21: Tidily
*Lot Fourteen* · Version 1.9 · EN

## Day Two Hundred and Thirteen · Monday 4 May

The front door of the house on the river is not locked, because a building that is winding up has men in it moving things and a locked door is a nuisance.

There is nobody at the desk where the visitors' book was. The book is on the counter with a pen beside it and nothing written in it since the twenty-ninth of April.

Georgij wrote his name in it anyway, and the time, and left the third column empty.

That is the third time he has written his name in a book at a door in eight weeks, and the first time nobody has been standing there to watch him do it.

The lights are on in one corridor on the first floor and off everywhere else, which is a thing a building does when there is one person left in it who is not paid by the hour.

Mr Hwang was in the room at the end with three crates open and a list.

He is about fifty. There is nothing in the room but the crates, a table and a chair, and he was standing.

"We are closed," he said, without looking up. "If you are from the fund you are two days early and I have not finished."

"I am not from the fund."

He looked up then.

"Then you have walked into a building that is shut and I have about six hours of work in front of me. Say what you want in one sentence and I will tell you whether I have got time for it."

"You have four entries on the back page of a catalogue you tidied," said Georgij. "All four were sold as deletions and all four were paid for. You found that out and you left them where they were."

Mr Hwang put the list down on the table.

"Sit down," he said. "There is one chair and you may have it, and I am going to stand, because I have been standing since seven and if I sit down now I will not get up again."

Georgij did not sit down either.

"You are correct," said Mr Hwang. "I want to say that first so that we are not doing the part where you prove it to me. I found it in the second week of December, in the settlement ledgers, and it took me about an hour."

"Four fees over four years," he said. "Three of them were in that hour. The fourth is dated the nineteenth of February, ten weeks after I stopped the practice, and I did not find it until the catalogue was already at the printer. Two of them are the same buyer. One is a woman who has bought here since I was a boy. One is a man."

"And there is a thing about the man that does not fit, and I am going to give it to you now, because you will get there eventually and I would sooner you got there from me."

"The thing that does not fit."

"He paid the fee. It is in the ledger with the other three and it is the same money in the same hand." Mr Hwang did not move. "But the lot itself never went through settlement at all. No invoice, no clearing, no line at that desk, nothing. This house let a lot walk out of the building and did not send anybody a bill for it."

"So he was not billed for the thing," said Georgij, "and he paid to have the record of it taken out."

"Yes."

"Those two do not go together."

"They do not go together at all, and I have had five months on it." Mr Hwang picked the list up and put it down again. "A man who is not billed is a man this house owes something to, or is frightened of, or belongs to. And a man in any of those three positions does not have to pay anybody a fee. He can simply say take it out."

"And he paid anyway."

"He paid anyway, on the same terms as everybody else, in cash, through the same man." He looked up. "I have never been able to make that mean anything except one thing, and I do not like it."

"And what that means."

"That he did not want anybody in this building to know that he could have had it for nothing."

"And you did nothing."

"I did not delete them. That is not the same as nothing and I am not going to let you have it as the same." He said it quite steadily. "I stopped the practice on the day I found it, and it was sold once more after that, and I have put that in front of you before you asked me for it. It has not been sold since the man who sold it walked out of this building. That is the whole of what I was brought here to do. I did it in nine weeks and it took ten more before it was true."

"What you did about the four."

"Nothing," said Mr Hwang.

The building did what an empty building does.

"Then that is the thing I have come about," said Georgij. "Not the practice. The four."

"They paid for a service," said Mr Hwang. "The service was not performed. I have been aware of the shape of it since December and of the last of them since the end of February, and I made a decision and I have not changed it. If I delete an entry because somebody paid for it to be deleted, then I am a man who deletes entries when there is a reason, and there is always a reason."

"That is a very good sentence," said Georgij. "I would like to take it apart, and it is going to take about a minute, and you are going to be able to follow all of it."

"Then take it apart."

"The rule you were brought here to hold is that this house does not sell deletions." He kept his hands at his sides. "It is a rule about the future. It is a rule about what you accept money for from tomorrow onwards. It has nothing whatever to say about four people who paid for something last year and did not get it."

Mr Hwang did not answer.

"You had three ways out of December and every one of them was clean," said Georgij. "You could have performed the four. You could have refunded them, in full, with a letter saying why. Or you could have told each of them exactly what had been done to them and let them decide."

"Yes."

"You took none of them. You kept the money and you kept the record. That is the position the men before you were in. The only difference between you and them on the thirty-first of December is that your filing is better."

Mr Hwang picked the list up again and then put it down without looking at it.

"That is not fair," he said.

"No," said Georgij. "It is accurate. Those are different words and I chose the one I meant."

"I could not perform them without becoming the thing I was sent to stop."

"You could not perform them. You could have refunded them in an afternoon, and it would have cost this house about a tenth of what it made from them. There is not one sentence in your rule that says a house may keep money for work it did not do." Georgij did not raise his voice at any point. "You did not decline to delete four entries. You declined to give four people back a thing they had already bought, and you called that a principle."

The room was very quiet.

"You have not been running a clean house for five months," he said. "You have been running the same house tidily."

Nobody in that building had ever said it to him, because everybody in that building had thought he was the improvement.

Mr Hwang stood with one hand on the edge of the table for what was probably eight seconds.

"There is a rest of it," he said. "You did not come here to give me a lecture on obligations. There is a fifth thing and you have been holding it since you came through the door."

"On the fourteenth of March one of those four entries was photocopied and sent to a woman in Ulsan who had nothing," said Georgij. "By the twenty-third of April she had lost the chair of her association. By the middle of this month she will have no firm. She is fifty-eight and she has never told an untruth in her life and she has two trucks left."

"And the page that did that," said Mr Hwang.

"Is on the back of the catalogue you built. You put the four retained entries on one page because a thing that cannot be found goes wrong later, and you were right about that too." He looked at him. "It has been posted to every buyer this house has. It went to six hundred and forty addresses in the first week of March. It cannot be collected."

Mr Hwang sat down on one of the crates, which is not a chair, and put his forearms on his knees.

"Who are you?"

Georgij told him, and gave him the whole of it, which is a thing he has done four times since October.

He watched the name go in and he watched what it did, and it took about two seconds, because the man in front of him has read those four entries more carefully than anybody alive.

"Lot fourteen," said Mr Hwang.

"Yes."

"The fourth of October. Struck on the nineteenth of February." He said it the way a man reads out a shipping mark. "And retained. And I retained it."

"You retained it."

Mr Hwang looked at the floor of a room with three crates in it.

"Is the house shut because of you," he said.

There it was, and it was a direct question from a man who does not ask any other kind.

"Yes," said Georgij. "Not by me. I told one customer the truth about what had been done to her, in one sentence, in her own house, in March. She checked it in a catalogue she already had. Everything after that was hers and I have not spoken to her since."

"And you knew what she would do."

"I knew exactly what she would do. That is why I said the sentence."

Mr Hwang nodded slowly, once, and did not say anything about it at all.

"There is one more thing and it is not an argument," said Georgij. "It is a fact and you have not got to it yet, and I would rather you had it from me standing in this room than worked it out in June."

"Then the one more thing."

"You are finished."

"Not the house. You." He did not decorate any of it. "You are the most honest man in this trade and you have five months on your record and a building that died under you. Nobody in this country is going to read that charitably and nobody is going to ask. In eleven years, when somebody says your name, the sentence after it will be the name of this house."

Mr Hwang sat on the crate with his forearms on his knees and did not move.

"I did the job," he said.

"You did the job. That is the part I cannot get past, and I have been trying since the twenty-third of April." Georgij waited for him to look up. "Nobody in the whole of this took a single won. Not you. Not me. Not her. Everybody involved did what they thought was correct and a woman of fifty-eight is going to be selling two trucks on Thursday."

That is the arithmetic he has been carrying since April, and there is nobody in it to be angry with.

Nobody said anything for a while.

"You want something," said Mr Hwang. "You have not asked for it yet and you have been in this room for twenty minutes."

"Yes."

"Then ask, because I have got about four hours left in me and I would like to spend some of them on the crates."

"The four fees," said Georgij. "Somebody in this house took them. Four times over four years. That man had a name and a position and he signed something each time."

"Yes."

"I would like it."

Mr Hwang did not answer for a moment, and it was not reluctance and it was not calculation.

"You understand that I have spent five months not being the sort of man who does that."

"I understand that you have spent five months not doing a number of things," said Georgij, "and that we have just been over what the last one cost."

That landed, and it landed properly, and Georgij watched it land.

Mr Hwang got up off the crate and went to the table and wrote on the back of the list. He wrote for about fifteen seconds, which is longer than a name.

Then he tore the strip off and held it out. He did not put it down on the table to be picked up, which is a thing a man does when he wants it clear that he handed it over.

"A name, a position, and the dates of the four," he said. "He left at the end of February, a week after the last of them went through, and I have never been able to decide whether those are two facts or one. He told the payroll office he did not want to work for a fund."

"Where is he now?"

"On the second line."

Georgij looked at it.

"Thank you."

"Do not." Mr Hwang went back to the crates. "I have just done in twenty seconds the thing I refused to do for four people in five months. I did it because a man came in here and made me feel it." He did not turn round. "I would like to be quite clear with myself about what that says."

Georgij stood in a room with three crates in it and did not have an answer for that either.

At the door he stopped.

"Mr Hwang."

"Yes."

"You will not be given another house," said Georgij. "You are going to be given work by somebody eventually and it is going to be beneath you, and you are going to take it, and you will do it properly because you cannot do anything the other way."

"Is that supposed to be a kindness?"

"No. It is the last true thing I have got and I have run out of the other kind."

He wrote the time in the second column of the visitors' book on the way out, because there was nobody there to do it. The book will be in a crate by Friday and nobody is ever going to read either line.

---

# Book Two · Chapter 22: I did not offer you anything
*Lot Fourteen* · Version 1.8 · EN

## Day Two Hundred and Fifteen · Wednesday 6 May

Mr Byun kept the register of that house for twenty-six years and left it at the end of February, ten weeks after the fund completed. He did not want to work for people who would ask him what he did all day.

He is sixty-eight. He lives on the eighth floor of a building in Seongdong with a view of the river that he paid about forty per cent extra for. He told Georgij about the forty per cent inside the first two minutes.

He opened the door himself and was pleased to have a visitor.

That is the part Georgij had not prepared for and it cost him about half a minute to adjust to.

"You are from the fund," said Mr Byun. "You are the fourth one and I have told the other three everything I know, which is a great deal, because I was in that building longer than any man alive."

"I am not from the fund."

"Then you are from the auditors. Sit down. Do you want tea, I am not going to make it but I can offer it."

"I am from one of the buyers," said Georgij.

He got a small pause for that and then a completely open face.

"Which one. I had two thousand of them."

"Four of them paid you to have an entry deleted," said Georgij, "and you took the money and did not do it. October of last year, February of this year, and two others going back four years."

Mr Byun sat down on his own sofa and looked at him.

He was not frightened, and he was not angry, and there was one thing that happened on his face and it was not either of those.

He was trying to remember which four.

That is the moment Georgij will not be putting down for some time.

"The February one," said Mr Byun eventually. "That was a woman. Very direct. She came four times and on the third occasion she did not bring money, and I have thought about that visit since, because she was the only one of them who frightened me."

"And the others."

"The October one is the same woman. That one was easy, that one was a withdrawal before the sale and those are nothing." He waved a hand. "The other two are further back and I do not have them by heart."

"One of them was Mrs Sunwoo."

"Yes." He nodded, pleased. "Yes, that is right. Three years ago. Charming woman, very old family. She sent somebody with it in an envelope and I never saw her at all."

Georgij did not say anything for a moment.

"You do not appear to be worried," he said.

"Should I be worried."

"You took money for a service four times and did not perform it."

"I took money for a service that this house had been selling since before I sat down in that chair," said Mr Byun, and he said it comfortably and without any defensiveness at all, "and I did what was done. I did not invent it. The man before me did it and the man before him. It is the only thing that house had to sell that nobody could get anywhere else."

"And the not performing it."

"Nobody was hurt," said Mr Byun.

The river did whatever the river does eight floors down.

"There is a woman in Ulsan called Nam Byung-hee," said Georgij. "She is fifty-eight. On the fourteenth of March somebody sent her a copy of the page that has those four entries on it, and she used it. By the middle of this month she will have sold four trucks and lost a firm her brother left her."

Mr Byun looked politely interested.

"That is very unfortunate. I do not know her."

"No. She does not know you either."

"Then I am not sure what you are here for."

"I am here to tell you what is going to happen," said Georgij, "and then I am going to leave, and there is nothing in the middle."

"The four buyers are going to be told." He did not raise his voice at any point. "By name. Yours. What each of them paid, which afternoon they paid it on, and that the entry is still there. One of them is the woman who frightened you and one of them is Mrs Sunwoo, and what any of them does after that is theirs and not mine."

Mr Byun did not move for about four seconds.

Then he got up off his own sofa and stood in the middle of his own sitting room with a view he paid forty per cent extra for.

"That is not necessary," he said.

"No."

"I can give it back. All four. It is not a great deal of money and I have got it."

"I know you have got it."

"Then let me give it back."

"They are still going to be told," said Georgij.

Mr Byun stood there.

"You cannot do that. I live here. My daughter-in-law's family is in this building." He had lost about eleven years off his voice. "Mrs Sunwoo knows everybody. Everybody. She will have it round this city in a fortnight and I will not be able to go to anything."

"Yes."

"What do you want?"

"I have not asked you for anything," said Georgij.

"Everybody wants something."

"I came here to tell you what is going to happen to you and I have told you." He stood up. "I would have been prepared to hear anything you said while I was in the room. I am going to be out of it in about a minute and after that I am not going to answer the telephone."

Mr Byun went and stood at the window.

"The fourth one," he said. "The man. You said four and you have named two of them and you have not named him, so you do not have him."

Georgij did not answer that at all.

"He is not like the others," said Mr Byun. "I want that considered. I want it taken into account that I am telling you and that I did not have to."

"Nothing is going to be taken into account. I am not trading with you and I want that said before you say another word, because if you say it thinking that you are buying something you are going to be angry with yourself tomorrow."

Mr Byun said it anyway.

"I did not take money from him."

He turned round from the window.

"Three of them came to me. The woman twice, and the old lady's man with the envelope. That is how it worked and that is what I did for twenty-six years." He had both hands on the back of a chair. "The fourth one did not come to me at all. I was told."

"By whom."

"By the owner. Personally, in his room, standing up, and it took under a minute and he did not sit down and neither did I."

Georgij stood very still.

"The whole of it."

"He said there was a lot going out that evening and there would be no invoice for it. I was to enter it and take it out again in the spring, and I was not to write anything at all about who had it." Mr Byun's voice had gone flat, which is what happens to men of that sort when they get to a thing they have kept. "And then he said the part I did not understand and have not understood since. He said the fee had been paid and I was to put it through the book as though it had come to me."

"He gave you the money."

"He gave me the money. In the room. From his own pocket, in an envelope that had already been made up." Mr Byun looked at the carpet. "I have taken cash from a great many people in that building and every single one of them wanted something for it. That is the only time in twenty-six years that anybody has ever given me money so that the money would be in the right place."

The flat was very quiet.

It is the one part of that minute Mr Byun never understood, and it is the part Georgij came away with.

"You wrote something down," said Georgij.

"How do you know that?"

"Because you were frightened, and a frightened man of that kind writes one line and puts it somewhere and then does not look at it for four years."

Mr Byun went into another room and was gone for about two minutes, and came back with a folded sheet out of a diary.

One line, a date, and four words about where the instruction came from.

He held it out and Georgij took it and read it and folded it again.

"Now the four are still going to be told," said Georgij.

"You have got what you came for."

"I did not come for that. I did not know it existed until twenty minutes ago and I did not ask you for it." He put it in the inside pocket. "You offered it to me because you thought you were buying something. I told you before you opened your mouth that you were not, and you did it anyway, and that is the whole of what has happened in this room."

Mr Byun stood in the middle of his sitting room.

"Then you are a very cruel young man."

"No," said Georgij. "I have been in three rooms in the last three weeks and in two of them that would have been true. In this one it is not, and you have not got the first idea why, and I am not going to explain it to you."

He got as far as the door.

"Twenty-six years," said Mr Byun, behind him. "Do you know what that building was like when I started in it."

"No."

"Nobody does. That is what I am going to be left with."

Georgij stopped with his hand on the door and did not turn round.

"Mr Byun."

"What?"

"Mrs Sunwoo paid you to take an evening out of a book three years ago, and she has carried the word round with her ever since like a receipt." He said it perfectly evenly. "She is eighty-one. When I told her in March that it had not been done, she rang a bell and had a catalogue brought out of a drawer. She found the line with one finger and did not need to be shown which one."

"You will be able to tell her all about the building when she comes."

He had not decided any of it before he went up.

He went there with two things, which were four dates and an address. He had worked out on the stairs that there is nothing available that hurts a man of that sort except what other people think of him.

The rest of it he decided standing in a sitting room, in the four seconds after a man of sixty-eight had to try to remember which four.

That is what it is now. Nobody put a ceiling on it, nobody is going to audit it, and there is no room he has to walk into afterwards and say what it cost.

He went down eight floors and out onto a street by the river, and read the four words again in the car, and did not like where they pointed.

# Book Two · Chapter 23: Three of the four
*Lot Fourteen* · Version 1.7 · EN

## Day Two Hundred and Twenty-Two · Wednesday 13 May

He noticed it in the car before they were off the bridge on the sixth of May, and he has not been able to do anything about it since.

He stood in a sitting room in Seongdong and told a man of sixty-eight that the four buyers were going to be told.

There are four buyers and he can reach three.

The fourth is the man he is looking for.

That is not a technicality and he is not going to let himself have it as one. He said a thing in a room that will be three quarters true, and Mr Byun will go to his grave not knowing which quarter, and the only person who is ever going to notice is Georgij.

He wrote it in the notebook under the date, in four words, and did not soften any of them.

Mrs Sunwoo received him in the same room, at the same time of day, with the same lamp on.

She did not stand up this time and she said so.

"I stood up in March because I did not know what you were and it seemed safer. Sit down and tell me why you have come back, and do not do the thing where you say one sentence and stop, because I am eighty-one and it was charming once."

"His name is Byun," said Georgij. "He kept the register for twenty-six years and he left at the end of February. He took your money in an envelope from a man you sent, three years ago, and he did not do the thing you paid for and he did not intend to."

Mrs Sunwoo sat very still.

"And the rest."

"There were four of them and you are one. He could not remember which four when I put it to him, and he was not being difficult about it. He was trying."

She did not say anything for a while.

"Where is he," she said.

"Eighth floor of a building in Seongdong with a view of the river that he paid forty per cent extra for. His daughter-in-law's family is in the same building."

"That was more than you needed to tell me."

"Yes."

She looked at him for a moment.

"You are inviting me to do something."

"I am giving you a fact that belongs to you and that I obtained without asking your permission, and I would have brought it to you if there had been nothing at the end of it at all. What you do is yours. I have not got a view and I would not give you one if I had."

"That is exactly what you said in March," said Mrs Sunwoo, "and it was true in March as well, and I have not decided yet whether that makes it better."

She rang the bell and asked for the diary.

"I am going to be very slow about this," she said, when it came. "It will take about three weeks and it will not involve one raised voice or one untrue word, and at the end of it he will not be asked to anything for the rest of his life."

"Yes."

"You do not want to know how."

"No. I want you to be able to say afterwards that you did not tell me."

He had given her the address and the daughter-in-law's family without being asked for either, and then arranged not to know what she did with them.

Mrs Sunwoo wrote three names in the diary in a hand that has not changed since 1971.

"Two things before you go," she said. "The first is that the house on the river is finished and I did not do very much of that. Eleven people did it and I only had to be the first one to say it out loud, and I have been thinking about that since the end of April."

"The second."

"You did not come here in March to give me anything," she said. "You came here because you needed the house shut, and telling me the truth was the only way to get it, and both of those are the case at once. I worked that out in about four minutes after you left and I have never held it against you."

"No," said Georgij. "You should."

"I am eighty-one. I have not the time to hold things against people who tell me the truth. There are so few of them that I would run out of afternoons."

* * *

He told Annie on the Thursday, in the small room, standing, in the same form he had used with Mrs Sunwoo.

"You are aware that I already know all of this," said Annie.

"Yes."

"You have known me since October and you are standing at the corner of my own desk reciting my own dates back to me."

"Yes, Mistress."

"Then say why you are doing it, because you have a reason and I would like to hear it before I decide whether it is a good one."

"Because you are two of the four," said Georgij. "October and February. If I tell Mrs Sunwoo formally and tell you across a supper table, then you are a different sort of buyer from her, and you are not. You paid the same man the same money for the same thing and he did the same nothing with it."

Annie looked at him.

"That is a better reason than I expected," she said.

"There is a second one and it is worse."

"Go on."

"I told a man in Seongdong that four people would be told. I can reach three." He said it flatly. "Doing all three properly is the only part of that sentence I have any control over, and I would rather do the part I can than decide that the whole thing was approximate."

She did not answer that immediately.

"Sit down," she said. "You have been standing in doorways for a week and it is beginning to look like a position."

He sat down on the floor at the side of the desk.

* * *

"Now the other thing," said Annie. "You have had it since Wednesday and you have not brought it to me, and that is not the arrangement, because there is not an arrangement any more and you know exactly what I mean."

"The owner," said Georgij.

"The owner."

He got the notebook out and did not open it, because he has had it by heart since the seventh.

"The house had one owner from 2011 until the winter," he said. "A man called Yeom. He is sixty-three. He did not build it and he did not particularly want it. He ran it the way a man runs a thing he inherited, which is to say he did not look at it very much and it made money."

"And in the winter."

"In the winter he sold it to the fund."

"And he took a position with them," said Annie.

Georgij looked up at that.

"You knew."

"I did not know. I have watched four men sell four things to four funds since I was twenty-six, and three of them took a position. A fund does not want the building. It wants the man who knows what is in it." She was not being clever about it. "Say where the position is."

"An address in Jung-gu," said Georgij. "Third floor. There are ten companies registered at it and none of them has any staff."

The clock in the hall did the thing it does.

"That is the address," said Annie.

"That is the address I stopped at on the night of the sixteenth of March, at twenty past one. I did not order the filings for it. I did not send for the register extract, and I left the whole of it exactly as I found it."

"And you were right to."

"I was right to. It was the correct thing and I have not changed my mind about one part of it." He put his hands flat on the floor beside him. "And the man who told Byun to put a lot through the book without an invoice is sitting on the third floor of it, and has been since January."

Annie did not say anything for a long moment.

"Say what you want to do," she said, "and do not put it as a question, because you decide these now and I am not going to let you make me do it by asking."

"I want to go at the address."

"Then say the thing you are not saying."

"The last time I stood in front of that structure I behaved correctly," said Georgij, "and behaving correctly in front of a man who reads arrangements is the same as signing my name, and you told me that in December and again in March and you were right both times. Backing away was invisible. Going at it will not be. There is no version where I do this and stay the man he cannot see."

"No."

"So the question is not whether it is dangerous. It is whether I am prepared to stop being the only thing about me that has been useful since March."

Annie got up and went to the window.

"You have had ten weeks of being the one man in Seoul he cannot see," she said, "and it has bought you a woman in Ulsan, a broker in Jung-gu, a registrar in Seongdong and a house that no longer exists. Say what it has not bought you."

"Him."

"It has not bought you him. It was never going to." She turned round. "Invisibility is a thing you spend. It is not a thing you keep, and a man who keeps it for ever has spent his whole life not being seen and has nothing at the end of it except that."

Georgij sat on the floor and did not move.

"That is not permission," he said.

"No. It is not permission and it is not an instruction, and you are going to have to decide it, and you are going to have to do it in a room with nobody in it but you." She came back to the desk. "But you asked me a fortnight ago to put the ceiling back on and I said no, and I am not going to spend the first difficult one pretending I have not got an opinion."

"You have got an opinion."

"I have got an opinion, and it is that you have been carrying a very expensive thing around for seven weeks in case it came in useful, and that it is the fourteenth of May and it has not."

He sat with that for a while.

"There is one more thing you should have before you decide," said Annie. "It is not going to help and I am going to give it to you anyway. It is the second piece I have taken off that shelf since December, and I would like you to notice that I am counting."

"I have noticed."

She was naming the price before she paid it, which is the rule she had put on him in March.

"The man you are looking for does not own anything at that address either," she said. "Not one share of one company on that floor. He is not on any of it and he never has been."

"Then what is he."

"He is the reason ten companies with no staff are on the third floor of a building in Jung-gu," said Annie, "and there is no document anywhere in this country that says so, and there never will be, and that is what you are proposing to walk towards."
