*And I have just found out what I bought with them, and it was a Saturday morning with twelve stems on my desk and her name at the gate for the first time this year.*

---

# Book Two · Chapter 48: The one who does not leave
*Lot Fourteen* · Version 1.2 · EN

## Day Two Hundred and Ninety · Monday 20 July

Jang had given him the other word on the Friday, and then Saturday had happened, and the flowers had taken up the whole of a weekend that the word should have had.

He had it written down twice, once in Jang's phrasing and once in his own, because he had learned in June what happens to a fact that gets tidied before it is used.

*Certain. Nine on the rota, counted eleven mornings across six weeks, never once ten. The Friday order has fed ten every Friday since the summer four years ago and nine every Friday before it. The grocer has not changed his round, his prices or his handwriting in six years.*

Jang had said one thing more on the telephone and had made a point of saying it slowly.

"I am giving you certain about a quantity," he had said. "I am not giving you certain about a person. I have never seen a tenth person, and I want that in whatever you write down, because in a year somebody is going to read your book and not mine."

* * *

Sang-hoon took a table again rather than a room, and this time Georgij understood it as the compliment it had turned into.

"You have had three weeks," said Sang-hoon.

"I have had three weeks and I have an answer, and it is not the one you asked me for." Georgij sat down without being asked, which he had not done in eight months. "You asked me whether the woman Jang has been watching is the same woman the trust was built for eleven years ago."

"I did."

"I do not know. I have not got one document that touches it and I am not going to guess at it in front of you." He put both hands on the cloth. "And it has stopped being the question."

Sang-hoon put his cup down.

"Say why."

"Because there are two of them in that house."

The restaurant went on being a restaurant, which is the only reason either of them chose it.

"Say how you know that."

"Nine people work that building on a rota. Four cars, two of them carrying two, counted on eleven separate mornings across six weeks by a man who never once went through the gate." Georgij did not hurry any of it. "The grocer delivers a standing order every Friday. It feeds ten. It has fed ten every Friday since the summer four years ago, and it fed nine every Friday before that, and it has never once gone back down."

"That is food and not a person."

"That is what Jang said, in those words, and he made me repeat it back to him before he would hang up." Georgij let that stand for a moment. "It is a quantity in the shape of one person, which arrived in the summer four years ago and has not left since. In the same summer a doctor drove a very long way to a house in Gangwon-do and put a lot number in the box where a patient's name goes."

Sang-hoon did not say anything at all for a while.

"You are telling me," he said eventually, "that the person you have been looking for since May is in that building."

"I am telling you that somebody has been in that building for four years who did not arrive in one of the cars and does not leave in one of them." Georgij put one hand flat on the cloth beside the cup. "I have wanted it to be her since Friday afternoon and I have written that down twice, in two places, so that it cannot quietly become evidence."

"That is a very careful sentence."

"It is the only careful thing I have left. I have been loud for five weeks and I would like one part of this to still be worth something in September."

Sang-hoon sat back.

Then he did the thing that Georgij had not planned for, and had not planned for because it had not occurred to him that the man was capable of it.

"Give it to me," said Sang-hoon.

"Say what you mean."

"I mean the house. I mean the woman at the window and whoever else is in there." He said it quietly and without any performance in it at all. "I have people. Real ones, not men who stand on roads. I have lawyers who can be at a district office at nine in the morning with a welfare application, a doctor and a court officer. I have enough money to make a provincial authority move in a week instead of a year. You have a notebook and a man with a folded map."

Georgij did not answer straight away.

"You would do that," he said.

"I would have it done by Thursday." Sang-hoon turned his glass a quarter turn and left it. "I have sat at that man's table for eight years and given away four things I cannot account for. I would like to take one out of the middle of him, and I would like it to be a person and not a document. I am fifty-nine and I have not wanted anything that specific in a long time."

It was the first entirely honest offer anybody had made Georgij all year, and he had to say no to it, and he took a moment before he did because it deserved one.

"No," he said.

"Then say it properly. Not the polite version."

"If your lawyers walk into a district office on Thursday morning, that building is empty by Friday night." Georgij put one finger on the cloth. "Not the woman. She cannot be moved quickly and a man who has kept her alive for eleven years is not going to kill her in a hurry. The other one goes. The one who did not arrive in a car, who exists on no paper anywhere in this country, who cannot be reported missing by anybody because there is nobody who has her name."

Sang-hoon did not move.

"You are saying I would rescue one and lose the other."

"I am saying you would rescue the one who has a name in a letterbox in Seodaemun and a trust behind her and eleven years of paper." Georgij heard his own voice go somewhere flatter than he had intended and let it. "And the one nobody can prove exists would be in a car within a day. There is not a court in this country that will order a search for a person who has no line, no owner and no date."

The words came out of him in that order because they are the order he has used about himself three times this year, and he heard it happen, and he did not correct it.

Sang-hoon heard it too.

"That is your own sentence," he said.

"It is."

"You have used it about yourself. In a shed, in May, and I did not say anything at the time."

"I know. I have used it three times and I noticed the second time and I went on using it." Georgij put his hands flat. "It is accurate. That is the only reason I have not stopped."

Neither of them said anything for a moment.

"Then what do I do," said Sang-hoon, "because I am not going to sit in a restaurant for the rest of the summer being told about a building."

"You do the thing you are the only person who can do, and it is not the house." Georgij took the folded sheet out of his inside pocket at last and put it on the table without opening it. "Baek Jun-ho has administered that trust for eleven years and eleven others besides. He is a solicitor with a practising certificate, which is more than that man has ever had, and it is the only thing in the entire structure that belongs to somebody who could lose it."

Sang-hoon looked at the folded sheet and did not touch it.

"You want me to frighten a lawyer."

"I want the opposite of that, and I am going to be exact about it, because if you get this wrong it is the same as the district office." He did not raise his voice. "I want to know what he has signed and what he thinks he has been signing. Not to threaten him with it. A man who has approved invoices for eleven years without asking has an explanation he has been living inside, and there is a version of Thursday where somebody sits down with him and finds out what it is."

"And if he goes to Choi Dae-ho the same afternoon."

"Then we find out that he already knew, and that is worth having and it costs us the trust." Georgij let it sit. "I am not going to pretend that is a small risk to hand you. It is the largest one I have asked anybody to carry this year and it is not mine to carry, and I would like you to sleep on it rather than answer me at this table."

Sang-hoon looked at him for a long moment.

"You have got worse at making things sound easy," he said.

"Yes."

"Good."

It was the whole of what he thought of the afternoon, and he had put it in one word so that it could not be argued with.

* * *

Annie was in the small room when he got back, at his desk rather than at hers, with the twelve stems still in water on the corner where they had been since Saturday.

She had the notebook open, which she does not do, and she had it open at the second page, which she has never done.

"You left it out," she said.

"I did." He stopped in the doorway. "Not on purpose. I would like that to be true rather than clever, so I am saying it before you ask."

"I know it was not on purpose. You have not done anything on purpose since Saturday morning." Annie turned the notebook round. "Sit down and tell me about Park Sang-hoon."

He told her, in order, and it took under four minutes, and she did not interrupt any of it.

"He offered," she said, when he had finished.

"He offered, and he meant it, and he would have had it done by Thursday."

"And you said no to the only offer of real help anybody has made you since October."

"Yes."

Annie put one hand flat on the open notebook.

"Say it out loud, the whole of it, because you have been carrying it since two o'clock and you have not put it down anywhere."

Georgij sat with that.

"There is a woman in a house in Gangwon-do who has been dying by nine days at a time since the spring," he said, "and a man offered me a court officer and a doctor on Thursday morning, and I said no, and the reason I said no is somebody I have never met and cannot prove is there."

"That is the whole of it."

"That is the whole of it. And I would do it again on Thursday, and again the Thursday after that, and I am not going to dress it up as a hard decision made well." He looked at the flowers rather than at her. "I chose the one nobody can see. That is the choice. There is not a second half to it that makes it better."

Annie did not tell him he was right, which he noticed, and which he was grateful for in a way he did not examine.

"You have not slept since Friday," she said instead.

"No."

"Then go up."

He got as far as the door.

"May I say one thing first?"

"You may say anything you like in this room. You have never once needed to ask that and I have never worked out whether you know it."

Georgij stood with his hand on the frame and found that the sentence he had been carrying up from the car was already halfway out of him.

"When he offered," he said, "I did not think about the house first."

Annie waited.

"I thought that if I gave it to him it would be finished. And if it were finished I would have nothing to bring up those stairs in the evening, and I had that thought before I had the one about the person in the building." He heard it land in the room and did not take it back, and then he stopped, which he does not usually manage. "That is as far as that goes tonight."

The room did the thing it does.

"Then that is as far as it goes tonight," said Annie.

She did not move from his desk and she did not close the notebook, and she did not say any of the four things she could have said, all of which he would have believed.

"Go up, Georgij."

He went up.

He did not write anything in either page that night, for the first time since the eleventh of June. In the morning he did not put a line through the gap or explain it. A book with an entry for every single day is a book somebody is writing for an audience.

---

# Book Two · Chapter 49: What he asked her
*Lot Fourteen* · Version 1.4 · EN

## Day Two Hundred and Ninety-Two · Wednesday 22 July

He went back to Mrs Bae on the Wednesday, in the afternoon, at the hour when the front of a restaurant belongs to whoever is standing in it and nobody else.

Annie had not told him to go and had not told him not to, and had said one sentence about it at breakfast which he had thought about the whole way there.

"You are going because it is correct," she had said, "and it is correct, and it is also the third time this month you have gone somewhere because the alternative was sitting in this house knowing about it."

Mrs Bae saw him through the glass before he reached the door, and did not look surprised, and did not look pleased.

"You have come back," she said.

"I have."

"Then you know."

"I know that somebody rang him," said Georgij, "and that it was you, and I have not come to say anything about that, and if you want me to leave before I say the rest, say so now and I will."

Mrs Bae put both hands on the desk with the book on it and left them there.

"I would rather have the whole of it now."

"You are not in any trouble and you are not going to be." He stood on the customer side and did not lean. "There is nothing you have done that anybody could put in front of anybody. You told a customer of nine years that a stranger had asked about him. There is not a court, a newspaper or a person in this world who would call that anything at all."

"That is not what I have been awake about."

"No. I know it is not." He kept his hands at his sides. "You have been awake because you gave me something first and him something second, and neither of them felt like the wrong thing at the time, and both of them cannot be right."

Mrs Bae looked at him for a moment and then, for the first time, sat down.

"You are a strange sort of man to have in my building twice," she said.

"Yes."

"Sit down, then. I am not going to talk about this looking up at somebody."

She made tea neither of them drank, which is what people do when they need four minutes.

"I telephoned him on the Thursday," she said. "Not the day you came. The day after."

"Why the day after."

"Because on the Wednesday night I decided I was not going to, and I was very satisfied with myself about it, and then I woke up at four and I was not satisfied any more." She turned the cup a quarter turn and did not drink from it. "Nine years. He asked after my sister when she was ill. I do not know how he knew she was ill."

Georgij did not say anything to that, because there was nothing to say that would not have been a knife.

"What you said to him."

"That a man had come and described him, accurately, and asked me for the name on the booking, and that I had given it." Her chin was level. "All of it. I did not leave any of it out and I did not tell him I was sorry, because I was not going to be sorry to him about a thing I had done to him."

"That is more than most people manage."

"I have kept a book in pencil for twenty-two years. I do not need a lesson from you about telling people the truth in the correct order."

"No," said Georgij. "You do not."

She almost smiled at that and did not, and put the cup down.

"Now ask me the question you came for, because you have been in my chair for six minutes and you have not asked it, and I know what it is."

"What did he say?"

Mrs Bae took a moment, and when it came it came in order, the way it does from somebody who has been over it.

"He was quiet for about three seconds. I counted them afterward, lying there, because there was nothing else to count." She put one hand flat. "Then he thanked me. Properly, the way he does. He said I had done exactly the right thing and that he would have been sorry if I had not rung."

Georgij did not write it down.

"Then he asked me one question. Only one." She looked at the desk. "He asked me what the man had looked like."

Georgij sat very still.

"His words, not yours."

"He said: what did he look like. And I told him, and he said thank you." Mrs Bae lifted her hand and put it down again. "And then he asked whether my knee had been better this summer, because he asked about it in the winter, and I said it had, and he said he was glad, and he rang off."

The front of a restaurant with eleven tables did the ordinary things it does.

"That is the part," said Mrs Bae.

"I know."

"He was not pretending, and that is what I have been awake about, and I would like to say it out loud to somebody who understands what I mean." Her voice did not change at all. "He asked about my knee after I had told him a thing that must have frightened him, and he was not doing it to seem calm. He was glad about my knee. Both of those were the same man in the same minute."

"Yes."

"Then I have earned what he is, since you know."

Georgij thought about it properly, because she had earned an answer and because he wanted to hear whether it held when it was said aloud.

"He is a man who is kind to everybody who is not the point," he said. "For nine years you have not been the point. Nothing he has done in this room was for anything. That is why you would put your hand in a fire for him, and it is also why he is worth what he is worth to the man he works for."

Mrs Bae took that without flinching.

"And somewhere there is a person who is the point."

"There is."

"Is she alive?"

Georgij did not answer straight away, and the not answering went across the desk exactly as it was.

"I think so," he said. "I cannot prove it and I am not going to sit here and tell you a comfortable thing I cannot prove."

She nodded once, slowly.

He had two more things to say and he said them standing, because a man who is about to ask nothing should not be sitting down comfortably while he does it.

"If he rings again, tell him whatever he asks and do not be careful about it," said Georgij. "That is not a tactic and it costs me. It is what will keep this a thing that happened to him and not a thing that happened to you."

"And the second."

"You are the only person in this who has done anything twice." He said it flatly. "Everybody else in five weeks has told me one thing and gone back to their day. You told me, and then you told him, and both times you did it on your own and neither time did anybody make you. I would like it said in this room that I noticed."

Mrs Bae looked at him for a long moment.

"Do not come back here," she said. "Not because of any of this. Because you are going to want to, in about a month, when something has gone wrong and I am the only person in the city who will still talk to you. I do not want to be that for you."

"No," said Georgij. "You should not be."

"Then we understand each other."

At the door he stopped, which he does when there is one more thing, and she was already looking at him as though she had been waiting for it.

"He counted three seconds," he said. "You said you counted them afterward."

"I did."

"Then he took three seconds to decide what to ask you, and out of everything a man in his position could have asked, he asked what I looked like." Georgij had his hand on the frame. "He did not ask you what I wanted. He did not ask you whether I had given a name, or who I worked for, or whether I had been to any other kitchen, or whether I had asked about anybody besides him. He asked one question that only helps him."

Mrs Bae did not follow it, and said so with her face and not her mouth.

"He is not running anything," said Georgij. "A man running something asks four questions. A man on his own asks one."

* * *

He told Annie in the small room before dinner, in order, and it took under three minutes.

She listened to the whole of it and then went and stood at the corner of the desk where the twelve stems were, four days old now and beginning to be four days old.

"He asked about her knee," she said.

"He asked about her knee."

"Then you were right on Saturday and now you have got it from a second room." Annie did not touch the flowers. "He has not told anybody. He is standing in the middle of an eleven-year arrangement holding a thing that would cost him everything to hand over. He will go on holding it for exactly as long as he believes he can manage it by himself."

"That is a seam," said Georgij.

"That is a seam." She turned round. "And I would like you to say out loud, once, tonight, what you are going to do with it. You have known since Saturday and you have not said it, and I have watched you not say it for four days."

Georgij put both hands on the back of the chair.

"I do not know yet," he said. "That is the true answer and I would give you a better one if I had it."

"That is the true answer and it is not the whole of it."

"No." He looked at the flowers rather than at her. "The whole of it is that there is a man out there who has been kind to a woman about her knee for nine years. I am going to use that, and I have not worked out which end of it I am going to use."

Annie let that stand in the room for a moment.

"Write it down," she said.

"Which part?"

"That sentence, in those words, tonight, before you have had time to make it sound better." She picked her pen up and did not use it. "You have started writing the tidy version again. Twice this month. I am not going to keep noticing it out loud for you."

He wrote it before dinner, on the first page, in the words he had used, and did not improve it.

*There is a man who has asked a woman about her knee for nine years and meant it, and I am going to use it, and I have not decided which end.*

And underneath, because he had promised himself in June that the page would hold both halves.

*Mrs Bae, and I have taken her off page two and put her on the third list, and she is the only person on it who did something twice.*

*She has told me not to come back and she is right, for a reason I would not have thought of. She can see the month I am about to have more clearly than I can.*

---

# Book Two · Chapter 50: The one he kept
*Lot Fourteen* · Version 2.7 · EN

## Day Two Hundred and Ninety-Eight · Tuesday 28 July

Sang-hoon sent for him at ten in the morning, to his own office, which he has not done once in eight months.

The room is on the fourth floor and it is not the room a man of that size would be given by anybody who did not know him. It is not large. There is a window that faces a yard rather than a river, a desk that has been used, and two chairs on the visitor's side rather than one. Georgij noticed the second chair on the way in and understood it four seconds later.

The second chair had a man in it.

He was about sixty, in a suit that had been good eleven years ago and had been looked after since. He stood up when Georgij came in, which nobody in this country does for a man who arrives on foot.

"This is Baek Jun-ho," said Sang-hoon.

Georgij did not sit down.

He stood inside the door of a room on the fourth floor and did the arithmetic in front of both of them, and did not pretend he was doing anything else.

"You did not tell me," he said.

"I did not."

"Then before anything else happens in this room, I am going to say the thing out loud, because if I say it afterward it is a complaint and if I say it now it is a fact." Georgij kept his hands at his sides. "There are four people alive who could describe my face in connection with any of this. As of nine seconds ago there are five, and I did not choose the fifth, and the fifth administers that man's money."

Baek Jun-ho did not move at all.

"That is fair," he said, "and I would like to answer it, because it is about me and not about him."

"Then all of it."

"I have known since yesterday that this was going to happen and I have not told anybody, and I have had a night in which to." He said it evenly, in the voice of a man who has spent thirty years saying things in rooms. "I am aware that is not proof of anything. It is what I have."

Georgij looked at him for a moment.

Then he took the second chair.

Sang-hoon did it properly, which is to say he did not perform any of it.

"I went to him on Monday," he said. "In person, to his office, on my own, without an appointment, and I asked him one question and then I stopped talking, and I would like both of you to notice that I did not send anybody."

"The question," said Georgij.

"I asked him whether there was anything he had signed in eleven years that he had never been able to account for."

The room went quiet in a particular way.

"That is my question," said Georgij.

"It is your question. I have been sitting in it since the twenty-seventh of May and I have watched you use it twice, and I decided that a man of my age is allowed to learn something." Sang-hoon did not look pleased with himself. "It was Monday. It was my birthday. I did not want to spend the whole of it being sixty in a restaurant."

Neither of them said anything about that, which was correct.

Baek Jun-ho has administered eleven trusts for a firm in Yeouido for most of his working life, and one of them, for eleven years, is the one behind a property holding company in Gangwon-do.

"I will tell you what a trust of that kind is," he said, "because both of you have an idea of it and one of you has the wrong one, and I do not know which."

"All of it, then," said Georgij.

"It is a set of instructions and a bank account, and nothing else. My job is to do what the instructions say and to be able to show that I did." Baek had his hands on his knees. "I do not know who benefits from that trust, and I am not hiding it from you. I have never been told, and there is no legal reason anybody would have to tell me."

"What the instructions cover."

"The operating costs of a residence. Staff, provisioning, maintenance, utilities, insurance, and medical costs against invoice." He listed it the way a man lists a thing he has read four hundred times. "It is not an unusual instrument. I have three others that look very like it. In two of those the beneficiary is a child, in the third a man who cannot manage his own affairs, and all three families I have met."

"And this one you have not."

"In eleven years I have never met anybody connected with it, been to the property, or spoken to a person who has." Baek said it without any drama at all. "There is a correspondence address and there is a man who signs for the settlor, and I have dealt with him by letter and once, at the beginning, in a room."

Georgij did not move.

"What he was like," he said.

Baek thought about that.

"Extremely pleasant," he said. "He asked me about my practice for twenty minutes before we did any business, and he remembered my answers eleven years later, in writing, in a letter about something else entirely."

"Four years ago the instructions were amended," said Baek. "That is the part Mr Park asked me about, and it is the part I have not been comfortable with. I would like to be exact about the size of my discomfort. It is small, it has never kept me from sleeping, and it has never gone away."

"Say the amendment."

"A flat in Seodaemun was added to the schedule. Rates, service charge, standing utilities. Not rent, because it is owned outright." He kept his hands where they were. "There is nobody living in it. I know that because the utility consumption is what it is, and I see the figures every year, and a flat with a person in it does not use what that one uses."

"And you asked."

"I wrote once, in the ordinary way. I received a very courteous letter explaining that the property belonged to a member of the household who was being cared for elsewhere, and that her affairs were being kept in order against her return." Baek's voice did not change. "That is a perfectly good answer. It is the answer I would have given. I have been giving it to myself for four years."

Georgij put one hand flat on the arm of the chair, which was as much as he permitted himself.

"Against her return," he said.

"Against her return."

Georgij had been waiting for the schedule since the word amended, and now that he had it he did not ask for anything else.

He went the other way instead, which is the way he has gone in every room since June, and it works exactly once per man.

"In July, four years ago, that trust paid a medical invoice," said Georgij. "A house call outside Seoul. The travelling cost three times the attendance and it was settled inside the month."

Baek Jun-ho did not move.

"How do you know that?"

"Because a woman at a settlement counter passed it four years ago and has not had a comfortable hour since the ninth of January, and because it was paid." Georgij did not hurry any of it. "An invoice of that shape, against that address, in that month. There is exactly one account in this country it could have come out of, and you have just spent ten minutes telling me that you are the only man who signs on it."

Sang-hoon looked from one of them to the other and did not say anything.

"You have not asked me a question yet," said Baek.

"No. I am going to say a thing instead, and you will tell me whether it is true, and if it is not true I will have been wrong out loud in front of both of you." Georgij put one hand flat on the arm of the chair. "You kept a copy."

The room did not do anything at all for about four seconds.

"There is a reason under that."

"Because in eleven years you have queried one line, and it was the flat, and it was not that invoice." He kept his voice exactly where it was. "A man who queries nothing and is troubled by one thing does one of two things with it. He forgets it inside a year, or he takes a copy and never mentions it to anybody, and afterward he cannot explain to himself why."

Baek Jun-ho put both hands on the document case beside his chair, which had been there the whole time and which Georgij had not once looked at.

"And the reason you think it is the second one."

"Because you have not forgotten it. You are sitting in a room on a Tuesday morning with a man you had never heard of on Friday."

Nobody said anything for a moment.

"I paid it because it was properly rendered and inside the instructions," said Baek, "and because a solicitor who queries every unusual line in eleven years of a trust is a solicitor who does not have eleven trusts." He did not open the case. "And then I did a thing I have never done before or since."

"That is yours to say and not mine," said Georgij.

"I kept a copy."

There was a silence after that which Sang-hoon did not fill. Georgij let it run to the end of itself, because the next part had to be said by the man holding the case.

"You want it," said Baek.

"I do."

"Then there is what I get, and do not tell me that I get to do the right thing, because I have been doing the right thing on that account for eleven years and it has brought me here."

Georgij did not decorate it.

"You get to be told what you have been signing," he said. "I am the only person alive who can tell you. I have known since the second of June and it has been in a locked drawer since. I am going to tell you whether or not you open that case, because you earned it by sitting down."

Baek looked at him for a long moment.

"That is a strange way to negotiate," he said.

"It is not a negotiation. I am saying both halves at the same time so that neither of us has to pretend it is one." Georgij kept his hand where it was. "You have something I need and I have something you have wanted for four years. If I hand you mine first you will hand me yours, and I want both of us watching me do it in that order."

Baek Jun-ho opened the case.

He put it on the desk between the three of them, in a plastic sleeve, and did not hand it to anybody.

It is one page. It has a practice letterhead on it, and a date in July four years ago, and a line for the attendance and a line for the travelling, and the travelling is three times the attendance.

And in the box where the name goes there are six characters.

Georgij looked at it for a long time and did not touch the sleeve.

He has known what is on that page since the second of June. A woman at a settlement counter read six characters, put it through, and went to lunch, and has not stopped saying so since. He has been carrying her sentence for eight weeks.

This is the page.

"It is not a name, a hospital number or an insurance number," said Baek. "I have looked at all three formats for thirty years and it is none of the three, and that is as far as I have ever got with it."

"I know what it is," said Georgij, "and I said I would tell you first, so I am going to tell you before anybody in this room touches that sleeve."

"Then I will have it."

"It is a lot number."

Baek Jun-ho sat very still.

"I do not know what that means."

"It means that when that practice asked who they were attending, they were given a number instead of a name." Georgij put one finger beside the sleeve and did not touch it. "And that the number is the sort a house uses for a thing it is selling, and that the trust you administer paid the bill."

The window in that room faces a yard, and a yard on a Tuesday morning makes the noises a yard makes.

"I would like to sit for a moment," said Baek.

"Take as long as you want," said Sang-hoon.

He took about ninety seconds, and when he came back he came back all at once, which Georgij had seen once before this year, in a room with an exercise book in it.

"The flat," he said.

"Yes."

"The flat in Seodaemun is hers. Not the woman who is being cared for. The other one." Baek had gone entirely grey around the mouth. "Somebody has been having me pay the rates on a flat belonging to a person who was bought, so that the person would go on existing on paper."

A solicitor of thirty years got there out of one page and a utility bill, and he got there before the man who had brought him the page.

"I do not know that yet," said Georgij, "and I am not going to let you have it as a fact from me when it is a reading. I have two documents and a quantity of groceries."

"Do not do that." Baek said it quite sharply, and it was the first time his voice had done anything at all. "I am not a client and I am not a witness and you are not protecting me. I have signed that schedule every year for four years and I would like to be told what I have been signing, in the largest size it might be."

Georgij took that.

"Then the largest size is what you have just said," he said, "and I am not able to prove it, and I believe it."

There was one more thing, and it was Baek who raised it, standing, with the case under his arm.

"The man who signs for the settlor," he said. "You knew who he was before I described him. You had his face before I had finished the sentence."

"I did."

"Then you know something I have wondered about for eleven years, and I am going to ask it once and then let it go." Baek stood with his hand on the back of the chair. "Does he know?"

Georgij thought about the question properly, because it was the question, and because a man who had kept a copy for four years had earned an accurate answer rather than a quick one.

"I do not think he has been told," he said. "I think he has been given a version of it that a kind man could hold. I think he has held it, and that it has been made easy for him to go on holding it for a very long time."

"And you are going to take it off him."

"Yes."

Baek Jun-ho nodded once, the way a man does when something he has half known has been said in a room with other people in it.

"Then I am glad it is not me," he said, and went.

Georgij stayed behind for a moment, and Sang-hoon did not fill the silence, which he has learned to do since May.

"He kept a copy," said Georgij.

"He kept a copy for four years and did not know why." Sang-hoon turned his chair slightly. "I have four decisions I could not account for. He has one page he could not throw away. I do not think those are different things."

"No."

"Then say what you needed from this room, because you have had it since he opened that case and you have not said it aloud."

Georgij put both hands on the back of the chair he had not sat in when he came in.

"I needed the page," he said, "in the original, with a file reference on it, from a man who will say where he got it."

"For him."

"For him." Georgij did not decorate it. "There is exactly one thing on this earth that will move that man, and it is neither fear nor money nor anything that happens to him. It is finding out what the kind version was covering."

Sang-hoon looked at him for a while.

"Then get it in front of him," he said, "and do not do it in a restaurant."

# Book Two · Chapter 51: The sixth one
*Lot Fourteen* · Version 1.5 · EN

## Day Three Hundred · Thursday 30 July

The second delivery came on the Thursday, at the same hour as the first, to the same gate, and Mrs Seo did not carry it at arm's length this time. She carried it the way a woman carries a thing she has been half expecting for twelve days.

Twelve white stems. No wrap.

"There is a card," she said.

It is a plain card, the size the shops keep behind the counter, and it has four lines on it in a hand that has been taught rather than allowed to develop.

*Saturday. Eight o'clock.*

Then the name of a restaurant, and a district, and the words *the small room at the back*.

And underneath, on the fourth line:

*I have taken the room for the whole evening, so there is no hurry.*

No name. No initial. No question.

Georgij read it four times and did not touch anything else on the desk for a while.

He knew the restaurant before he had finished the second line, and knowing it was the whole of the message and everything else on the card was politeness.

There were six kitchens on the list he had made on a Sunday evening in June. He went to five of them. He stopped at five because he had put a number on it in front of Annie and written it down. Stopping under a number is not the same as going over one, and he had written that as well.

*Five of six. The sixth is not cancelled, it is unspent.*

The card names the sixth.

Georgij sat with that for a long time, and he did not enjoy any part of it, and he made himself go through it properly rather than admiring the shape of it.

*He knows there were six. He knows which five. He has spoken to enough of them to be able to count. Then he has looked at what is left, worked out which one I was going to walk into next, and taken it for a whole evening.*

*He is not showing me that he is clever. He is showing me that he can count as well as I can, in the same trade, faster, and that he has been doing it for longer.*

Annie read the card without picking it up, twice, and put one finger on the fourth line.

"That is the sentence," she said.

"It is."

"Say it, because I want to hear whether we have got the same one."

"He has taken the room for the whole evening so that there is no hurry." Georgij had his hands on the back of the chair. "There is one reason a man books a room for a whole evening for two people. He does not know how long it is going to take, and he has decided that whatever it takes is what he is going to give it."

"That is a man who intends to talk."

"That is a man who has already decided to talk and is telling me so on a card, a fortnight after he found out I exist." He did not sit down. "And he is not asking me for anything in exchange, and he has not put his name on it, and he has not said what it is about."

Annie stood back from the desk.

"Then say the other reading, because there is one and you have had it since ten past nine."

"The other reading is that a man who has been useful to somebody dangerous for eleven years has more than one way of solving a problem. A room at the back with no hurry is also a room at the back with no hurry." Georgij said it without any weight on it. "I do not believe it, and I am going to say why, and then I am going to say the part where I could be wrong."

Georgij waited with the receiver against his ear.

"He asked Mrs Bae one question, and it was what I looked like. If a man in that position wanted the other thing, he would not need a room, a card, or a date. He would need an address, and he has had this one for twelve days."

Annie let that stand.

"And the part where you could be wrong."

"That I like the shape of it," said Georgij. "It is a beautiful piece of work and I have been admiring it since breakfast, and a man who is admiring a thing is not examining it. You have told me twice this month that I have started deciding what things are before I know."

"Three times," said Annie.

"Three times."

She did not tell him not to go, and he had known she would not, and he found that he had been braced for it anyway.

"You are going," she said.

"I am."

"Then here is what I want, and it is not a condition, because I am not going to start pretending I have a way of making you keep one."

"Yes, Mistress."

"Mr Ku takes you and Mr Ku stays outside for the whole of it, and he is not there to protect you, because he is a driver and a driver is not that." She had both hands at her sides. "He is there so that at eleven o'clock somebody in the world knows the difference between a conversation that ran long and one that did not end."

"Yes, Mistress."

"And you take nothing in your pockets that anybody could take out of them." Annie looked at the card. "Not the notebook, not the list, and not that page."

Georgij did not answer straight away.

"I need the page," he said.

"You need what is on the page. There is a difference and you have known it since the day you told me the difference between a struck line and a person."

He stood with that for a moment.

"A copy," he said. "One copy of the one page, in an envelope, and nothing else in the envelope, and it comes back with me or it stays on that table and I do not mind which."

"That is what I meant."

"And Baek Jun-ho does not find out that a copy left this house until after Saturday, because if it goes wrong he will hear it from me and not from a man in a restaurant."

Annie nodded once, and that was the whole of the negotiation.

* * *

He telephoned Sang-hoon on the Friday morning, because a man who has been told something in a room on Tuesday is owed the sentence that makes it wrong.

"You told me not to do it in a restaurant," said Georgij.

"I did."

"It is a restaurant. I have not chosen it and I am not able to change it, and I would rather you heard that from me on a Friday than worked it out afterward."

There was a pause on the line that was not the line.

"Say who chose it."

"He did. He has taken the room for the whole evening." Georgij stood in the corridor with the receiver against his ear. "It is the sixth of the six kitchens I made a list of in June. I went to five and stopped, and I wrote down that the sixth was unspent, and on Thursday morning a card arrived with the sixth on it."

Sang-hoon did not say anything for long enough that Georgij could hear the yard behind him.

"Then he has been counting you," he said.

"He has been counting me since about the fifteenth, and he has done it out of the same trade I was counting him from, and he was faster." Georgij did not decorate it. "I have had that in front of me since Thursday and I have not found a way to make it smaller."

"Do not make it smaller. You are going to need it exactly that size at eight o'clock tomorrow." Something moved on the other end, a chair. "I am going to offer you a thing and you are going to say no to it, and I would like to have offered it anyway."

"Offer it."

"I can have four men within a hundred metres of that door for the whole of the evening, and not one of them would come in unless the room went quiet."

"No," said Georgij.

"Say why, properly."

"Because he would know inside a minute." He kept his hand where it was. "That man reads rooms for a living and he has read that street before he booked it. If there are four strangers on it who were not there on Wednesday, he sits down at that table already knowing that I brought a crowd to a conversation. Everything I want out of that hour is gone before either of us has spoken."

"That is the answer I expected and I still wish it were the other one." Sang-hoon let it sit. "Then I will tell you the useful part instead, and it is not about tomorrow."

"The rest of that sentence."

"I have sat opposite that man once, at a table, and I did not know what he was, and I went home pleased." He said it flatly. "You are going to sit opposite him knowing exactly what he is, and you are going to go home in some state I cannot predict, and the difference between those two evenings is that you chose yours."

"Yes."

"Then whatever happens in that room, it is not the same as what happened in mine, and I would like you to have that in your pocket, since you are not taking anything else."

He spent Friday not preparing, which took more out of him than preparing would have.

He had learned that in December, in a car outside a house in Seongbuk, waiting to say four sentences to a man who ran a shipping line. A room where the other person has decided to talk is a room you can lose by arriving with a speech. There is no version of Saturday that goes well if he walks in having rehearsed the middle of it.

So he read the page again, twice, and did not write out a single sentence to say about it.

On Friday evening he did the one piece of preparation he permitted himself. It was a decision rather than a sentence, and he wrote it down so that it would still be there on Sunday, when he found out whether he had kept it.

*I am not going to accuse him of anything.*

*I am not going to tell him what he has done. I am going to put one page on a table and let a man who has been reading paper for thirty years read it, and I am going to say nothing at all until he has finished.*

*Everything I want out of that room depends on him getting there before I do.*

He looked at that for a while, because there was a second half and he had been not writing it since Thursday morning.

*And he is going to be pleasant to me. He is going to ask me something about myself, and he is going to mean it, and I am going to want to answer him.*

*That is the trap, and it is not one he has set. It is simply what he is.*

* * *

Mrs Seo put the second twelve stems in water beside the first twelve, without being told, on the corner of the desk in the small room.

The first lot are twelve days old now and are doing what flowers do at twelve days.

She did not throw them out either, and nobody in the house had told her not to, and Georgij noticed that on the Friday night and did not know what to do with it except write it down.

*Two dozen white stems on one desk, one lot dying and one lot not yet. A woman who has worked in this house for nine years has decided on her own that neither of them goes in the bin.*

*Everybody in this building has understood what those flowers are. Nobody has said a word about them to me except the two people who had to.*

---

# Book Two · Chapter 52: Against her return
*Lot Fourteen* · Version 1.8 · EN

## Day Three Hundred and Two · Saturday 1 August

He was already there.

He had been there since half past seven, according to the girl who took Georgij through. He had asked her about the walk from the station and had said the wrong tram number on purpose, so that she could correct him.

The small room at the back has one table, six chairs of which four had been taken out, a window onto a wall, and a screen that folds across the doorway and had been left open.

He stood up.

"Thank you for coming," he said. "I did not know whether you would."

He is not quite as old as the cook had said and not as tall as Mrs Bae's hands had suggested when she described him. He has a face that does what he tells it to and has been doing it for so long that Georgij could not have said, in the first ten seconds, whether anything on it was chosen.

"You have not eaten here before," he said. "The soup is the reason to come. I have ordered it for both of us and you are under no obligation to touch it."

"Thank you."

"You are welcome, and I would like to say the next part before the food comes, because it is easier standing up and I am about to sit down." He put one hand on the back of his own chair. "I have not told him. Not on the sixteenth, when I found out, and not since. I am telling you that first because it is the only thing I have that you would want, and because if I keep it until later it becomes a card I am playing."

Georgij stood very still.

"Then I will say mine," he said. "I have not told him either, and I am not going to, and not as a favour to you. There is nothing in this year that I want less than that man knowing where I have been."

"Yes," said Sim. "I thought that was probably the shape of it."

They sat down.

The soup came and it was as good as he had said, and neither of them touched it for eleven minutes.

"You have been in five kitchens," said Sim.

"Six now."

"Six now." Something went across his face that was almost amusement and did not stay. "I counted the five. I would like to know how you chose them, because I have been trying to work it out for a fortnight and I have not managed it, and I do not enjoy that."

"By how long the same cook had been in the building."

Sim sat back.

"Because a room that has kept its cook has kept its memory," he said.

"Yes."

"That is very good." He said it the way a man says it about a thing in his own trade, without any performance in it. "I would not have thought of it. I have spent thirty years being pleasant to kitchens and it never once occurred to me that it made me findable by them."

"It is the only thing about you that is findable at all."

"I know that now."

"Ask me what you came to ask," said Sim, "because you have not asked anything, and I have been waiting for it since the door, and I am beginning to think you are not going to."

"I am not going to ask you anything."

"Then the reason. I have thirty years of men not giving me one."

"Because everything I would ask you, you would have to decide whether to answer, and then we are two men negotiating over a table. I have done a great deal of that this year and it has never once got me the true version of anything." Georgij had both hands where the other man could see them. "I have brought one thing with me. I am going to put it down and I am going to say nothing at all, and you may read it or not read it."

Sim looked at him for a moment.

"That is a considerable risk," he said.

"It is the only one I have got that is not a trick."

He took the envelope out of his inside pocket, and it was the only thing in that pocket, and he put it on the table between the two bowls and took his hand off it.

Sim read it the way a man reads who has read paper for a living.

He read the letterhead first, then the date, then the two lines with the figures. Georgij watched him notice that the travelling cost three times the attendance, and watched him not react to it, because that part he had known.

Then he came to the box where the name goes.

He stopped.

Georgij said nothing, which was the entire plan, and it was very much harder than he had expected it to be.

Sim read the six characters. Then he read them again. Then he put the page flat on the table, squared it with the edge without appearing to know that he was doing it, and sat with both hands on either side of it.

The room did what a small room at the back of a restaurant does.

"That is a lot number," he said.

"Yes."

"From the house on the river."

"Yes."

"I have never seen one."

"Again."

"A bill. From that house, or to it, or about it. In eleven years." He had still not looked up from the page. "I pay in an envelope and I do not take receipts. I have not taken one in thirty years, because a receipt is a piece of paper with two names on it."

One finger moved a fraction along the edge of the page and stopped.

"That is the first thing you learn and it is most of the trade," said Sim. "I have spent thirty years making certain that nothing of this kind exists anywhere I could reach it. It appears that I was very good at it."

He did not look up.

"July, four years ago," he said. "I sent flowers on the sixth and the twenty-seventh of April that year. I have sent them twice a year since, in April and in October. In April she was told, and October was her mother's month. I was given both of those dates in a letter eleven years ago and never once a reason for either."

Georgij did not move.

"What you understood the arrangement to be," he said, and it was the only sentence he permitted himself in nine minutes.

"You will have to forgive me. I am going to be slower than you want." Sim moved his bowl an inch to the left so that it was not between them. "A lady who is not well. A house in the country, and good people in it. I chose the people myself and I went out twice to look at them, and nobody had asked me to do that."

He said all of it the way a man recommends a dish.

"And a gentleman who does not want it talked about. There is nothing shameful in that. I have done four of them and two were sad and none of them were wrong."

Georgij did not touch his own bowl.

"Twice in four years I was told she was worse. Both times by letter. Both times the letter asked that something be added to the household, and both times it was done inside the week." He looked up. "I was glad to. I would like you to have heard me say that part."

"What did you add?"

"The first time, a doctor." He put one finger beside the six characters and did not touch them. "The second time, a flat."

Georgij sat in a small room at the back of a restaurant and understood that he was watching a man arrive somewhere.

"The flat in Seodaemun," said Sim.

"Yes."

"I go there three or four times a year and I empty the letterbox, and I have done it since the summer four years ago. I was asked to do it in a letter which said that her affairs should be kept in order against her return." He said the phrase without any weight at all, the way a man says a sentence he has been carrying in his own handwriting. "There is a woman on the ground floor who grows things in pots. I have asked her about them every time I have gone, because she is on her own and nobody asks her anything."

"I have met her," said Georgij.

"I know you have. She told me." Sim did look up then. "She told me exactly what you looked like and exactly what you asked, and she did not leave anything out, and she was not frightened. I have thought about that a great deal in three weeks, because it is not how people are with me."

Georgij did not tell him why, and it was one of the two hardest things he did that evening.

"Whose flat did you think it was," he said instead.

Sim put both hands flat on the table on either side of the page.

"Hers," he said. "The woman who is ill. I have never once asked myself why a woman who has been in a house in the country for eleven years would have a flat that was added to the arrangement seven years after she went there."

Neither of them said anything.

"It is not hers," said Sim.

"No."

"It belongs to the person on that invoice."

"I believe so. I cannot prove it, and I have written down twice that I cannot, and I am not going to sit at this table and tell you it is proved."

"Do not do that." It came out of him at last, and it was not loud, and it was the first thing he had said all evening that had not been arranged. "I have spent thirty years being handed the version that is comfortable to carry. You are the first person in eleven years who has put a piece of paper in front of me and let me read it. Do not start being kind to me at the end of it."

He did not eat anything.

Georgij noticed it at about twenty past nine, and once he had noticed it he could not stop noticing it. The soup went cold in front of a man who has complimented a cook in every room he ever sat in. He had ordered it before Georgij arrived, and he had said it was the reason to come.

There is one other man in this story who does not eat in front of the person he is working on.

Georgij did not say that out loud. He wrote it on the back of the envelope afterward, in the car, and he has not decided yet whether it was a kindness or a failure of nerve.

"There is one more thing," said Georgij, "and then you have everything I have."

Sim did not tell him to stop.

"That house had no oxygen in it until the July on that invoice." He said it without arranging it at all. "A tank in a private house has to be told to the fire authority. The filing is one event. There is nothing before it. It has never been renewed as new and it has never been cancelled."

Sim did not move for a long moment.

"Eleven years of flowers," he said.

"Yes."

"And seven of them with nothing in that house at all." He was not asking. "No tank. No doctor. Nobody driving four hours to get there."

"Nothing that anybody is required to write down."

Sim put one hand flat on the table beside the page and left it there.

"She was not worse."

"I have not said that."

"You have not said a great many things this evening and I have understood every one of them." It came out level and it did not stay level all the way to the end. "Somebody arrived. Everything that was described to me as an illness arrived in the same month as the somebody. I put two of those things there myself, and I was glad to, and I have just said so out loud in front of you."

He had arranged that household for eleven years and had never once been given a reason to ask, and it took one page and nine minutes.

"You were not slow," said Georgij.

"Do not."

"I am going to, and then I will stop." He did not soften any of it. "A man who is told she is worse has an explanation for a doctor, a tank, four more staff and a flat. It covers every fact he can see. It is the only one he was ever offered."

"You will not stop in the middle. Half of this is worse than none."

"You did not fail to work it out. You were answered before you had a question."

Sim was quiet for about four seconds.

"That is the kindest thing anybody has said to me in eleven years," he said, "and you have made certain that it is also true, and I cannot get the two of them apart. I have been getting those two apart professionally since before you were born."

* * *

"I am not going to give you him," said Sim.

"I have not asked you for him."

"You have not, and you are not going to, and we both know that is a technique as well as a courtesy." He straightened the page again, a fraction, with one finger. "I will tell you why not, because you have earned the reason and not the thing. He took me out of a place I would not have got out of on my own. He did it before he needed me and he has never once mentioned it in thirty years, and I do not know whether that is because he is decent or because he knew he would not have to."

"Those look identical from where you are sitting."

"They have looked identical for thirty years," said Sim. "Tonight is the first evening they have not."

Then he straightened his cuff, which is a thing he does before he arranges something.

"I am going to give you something else."

"I have not asked for that either."

"No, and you are going to let me finish, because I have spent thirty years being the man who arranges things in every room he sits in, and I would like to do it once more this evening." He was entirely courteous about it. "You cannot add a doctor to a household from a table in Seoul. You cannot add a flat either. Somebody in that house takes the telephone call and says yes. Somebody in that house lets the man in at the gate."

Georgij kept both hands where they were.

"I have spoken to the same person for four years," said Sim. "About the heating. About whether the second bathroom was worth doing. About a woman I have never met, in a house I have never been to."

"That person is not him."

"That person has never been him, and has never once pretended to be, and would not know how." Sim took a pen out of his inside pocket, which is where the envelope had been in Georgij's. "I am going to write it down now, before eleven o'clock, because at eleven o'clock I am going to be a man who has had time to think about it."

He put one hand on the page and pushed it back across the table, and Georgij did not take it.

"Keep it," said Georgij. "It is a copy. There is one more and it is with the man who kept it for four years without knowing why."

Sim looked at the page for a long moment and then folded it once, along a crease it did not have, and put it in his inside pocket.

"What will you do," said Georgij.

"Nothing further tonight. I have already done the one thing I was going to do, and I did it before I could think better of it." Sim stood up, and put both hands on the back of his chair, and did not push it in. "Then I am going to go home and sit up. I keep everything. Eleven years of letters, and two of them said she was worse, and I am going to find out what else was in those two."

"And then."

"And then I will know how much of my life was a courtesy and how much of it was a method." He was entirely level. "I would like you to understand that I may find out that it was a method and go on anyway. Men do."

"I know they do."

"Yes." Sim almost smiled at him, and it was not the smile from Mrs Bae's front desk, and it was not a performance either. "You are the only person I have met in thirty years who would have said so instead of telling me I would not."

He picked up neither bowl and left both.

At the doorway he stopped, with the folded screen beside him, and he did the thing that Georgij had written down on Friday night and had not been able to prepare for.

"May I ask you one thing that is nothing to do with any of it," he said.

"You may ask."

"Are you all right?"

Georgij stood in a small room at the back of a restaurant with a cold bowl in front of him and found that he had no arrangement at all for that.

"No," he said.

"No," said Sim. "I did not think so."

He had paid at half past seven, before the meal, as he always does. The girl at the front told Georgij so on his way past, because she thought he would want to know that it was already settled.

---

# Book Two · Chapter 53: The one I did not say in May
*Lot Fourteen* · Version 1.5 · EN

## Day Three Hundred and Five · Tuesday 4 August

On the seventeenth of June he had written down that Mr Yeom would be told. Not that week, and not by a man with something in his coat, and not in the same month if he could help it.

He had helped it. It is August.

And the thing that had made the whole of it impossible in June has gone, because there is nothing left in that house to ask for. He has the name. He got it from a woman with a book in pencil and a card with four lines on it and a small room at the back of a restaurant, and none of it came out of Mr Yeom.

*I can go and give him something and want nothing, for the first time since I met him. That is the only reason today is possible, and it is not a virtue, it is a calendar.*

* * *

Mr Yeom was in the same room as in May, with the same table, and he did not look surprised at all.

"I wondered whether you would come back," he said. "I have been wondering it since about the end of May, and then in July I stopped, and here you are in August."

"I am sorry about the gap."

"Do not be. A man who comes back in a fortnight wants something." He was already reaching for the dishes. "Sit down. You will eat, because I am not going to sit here with a plate in front of me and a foreigner watching me use it."

Georgij sat down, and ate, and it was very good, and he let ten minutes go before he started, because a man of sixty-three who has made lunch is owed ten minutes.

"I have come to tell you three things," said Georgij, "and to ask you for nothing at all, and I am going to say that at the start rather than at the end, because at the end it sounds like a technique."

"I am braced for the first one."

"The telephone call four years ago. The man who told you it was good to see you again, and you had never met him."

Mr Yeom put down what he was holding.

"You have found him."

"I have met him. On Saturday, for two hours, in a room he took for the whole evening." Georgij kept both hands on the table. "That is not the thing I came to tell you. The thing I came to tell you is that the telephone call was not strange."

"That is a sentence with something under it."

"You have carried it for four years as a peculiar minute in a working life. A man rang, said a warm thing that made no sense, and asked you for a favour on behalf of somebody who would be grateful." He did not hurry it. "It is a method and nothing else. It has been used on a florist in Hyoja-dong, on a woman who has kept a restaurant book in pencil for twenty-two years, on a solicitor in Yeouido eleven years ago, and on you. And out of the four of you, you are the one it was used on least."

The room did what rooms do.

"That is not what I expected you to say," said Mr Yeom.

"No. It is worse than the thing you were braced for, and you should have it in the size it actually is."

"Worse how."

"Because it means you were not asked a favour by a stranger who happened to have your number." Georgij looked at him properly. "You were chosen, and worked at for one minute by a man who is extremely good at one minute. He needed only the one, because you do favours for people who ask you nicely. He knew that before he dialled."

Mr Yeom sat with both hands flat on either side of his plate for a while.

"I have told myself for four years that I did a stupid thing on a Tuesday," he said. "You are telling me that somebody had a look at me first and decided a Tuesday would do it."

"Yes."

He had known on the way over that this was what he was bringing. A man is owed the real size of it.

"Then the second thing, and do not stop to be careful with me, because I am sixty-three and I would rather have it in one go."

"The name you would not give me in May," said Georgij. "I have it."

Mr Yeom did not move at all.

"From where."

"From a woman who kept a booking book, six weeks ago, and she gave it to me because I described the man before I asked and everything I said was right." Georgij did not soften any of it. "She has not slept properly since. She telephoned him the next morning and told him what she had done, and he thanked her, and he asked her about her knee."

"Then it came out anyway."

"It came out anyway."

Mr Yeom looked at the table for a long moment.

"I have kept that name for four years out of a thing I have had since I was a young man," he said. "I have worked for seven people in my life and I have never handed one of them to anybody. I said that to you in this room in May and I was rather pleased with myself about it."

"I know. I remember exactly how you said it."

"And it turns out it did not hold anything up at all." He said it without any self-pity, which made it worse to sit opposite. "The thing went out through a woman with a book. My silence was not a wall. It was a decoration on a house with no door in it."

Georgij took a moment, because this was the one he had thought about most on the way over.

"No," he said.

"That is not a whole no."

"It held for four years, and it did not hold today, and those are two separate facts and only one of them is about you." He kept his voice exactly where it had been all lunch. "Mrs Bae had a telephone number because he books rooms. You had a name because a man once trusted you enough to give you one. She gave up a booking. You would have had to give up the only thing you have never done in forty years. Those are not the same size and I am not going to sit at your table and pretend they are."

Mr Yeom did not answer that, and then he pushed his plate an inch away from himself, which he had not done in May.

"Then let me do it now," he said. "It is worth nothing now. Ask me and I will say it, and it will cost me the same as it would have cost me in May, and at least it will have been for something."

"No."

"You are refusing a name you already have. That is not generosity, it is arithmetic."

"It is both, and I am going to say the arithmetic first so that you do not have to trust the other part." Georgij put one hand flat. "If you say it to me today, then in five years you are a man who broke it. That is what you will remember, and you will not remember that I already had it, because nobody remembers the part that lets them off."

Mr Yeom looked at him.

"And the other part."

"The other part is that it is the last thing in this business that belongs to anybody," said Georgij, "and I have spent five weeks taking things off people who did not know they were holding them, and I would like there to be one I did not take."

"There was a third thing," said Mr Yeom, after a while. "You said three."

"There is a third thing and it is the one I have been not saying since May."

"Then we have both been not saying it."

Georgij put both hands in his lap, which is not a thing he does.

He had never given anybody a date about himself. He was about to give one away for nothing.

"In May I told you that I work for the woman who owns the two entries. October and February." He said it evenly and did not decorate it. "That was true and it was chosen, and I chose it in your hallway before you opened the door, and I have thought about it every day since."

Mr Yeom went very still.

"There is a rest."

"I am the February one."

The room was quiet in the way it had not been all afternoon.

Mr Yeom did not say anything for a long time, and when he did his voice was not what it had been.

"You sat at this table in May," he said, "and let me tell you about a fee in an envelope."

"I did."

"And you did not say."

"I did not say, and I am not going to tell you it was tactics, because it was not." Georgij made himself finish it. "I do not give anybody dates about myself. It is the one rule I have had since I was nineteen and it has kept me alive in eleven houses. And in May I used it in your dining room on a man who was giving me the truth for nothing, and I have known since about the Thursday afterward that I owed you this sentence."

Mr Yeom stood up.

He went to the window, and stood there, and did not turn round, and Georgij let him have it.

"My father's house," he said, to the glass. "He ran it for thirty years and I have run it since the year he died, and I never once went down to the floor. I have said that in this room as though it were modesty."

"I know."

"And in October of last year a man went out of my building." He still had not turned round. "And in February my register was corrected for money by a man I had trusted for twenty-six years. I found out about one of the four and let it go in ten minutes, and the one I found out about was not you."

"No."

"Then which one did I hear about."

"The boy," said Georgij. "Lot eleven, in October. Byun came to you in February about that one because it frightened him, and it frightened him because of what the buyer wanted. Mine went through in the same seven weeks and he did not mention it, because mine did not frighten anybody."

Mr Yeom put one hand on the window frame.

"That is the worst sentence anybody has said in this house," he said, "and you said it as though it were an ordinary piece of information."

"It is an ordinary piece of information," said Georgij. "That is the whole of what I am trying to tell you about that building."

He came back to the table eventually and sat down and did not touch the food again.

"I am not going to apologise to you," he said. "You would not know what to do with it and I would not know how to make it the right size."

It was an apology with the word left out of it, and it was the largest one the man had.

"No. Thank you."

"So I am going to do the other thing." Mr Yeom put both hands on the table. "I took a position with the people who bought that house in December. It is not a large one and it is not honest work in the sense that it requires me to do any. I sit in two meetings a year and I have a folder sent to me every quarter and I have never once opened one past the first page."

Georgij did not say anything at all.

"I did not ask why they wanted the house," said Mr Yeom. "I have told you that already and I was comfortable about it for four years and I have not been comfortable since May. And you are not going to ask me for it, because you have made a great performance this afternoon of not asking me for anything, and I have watched you do it and I am not a fool."

"I am not going to ask you for it."

"I know. So I am offering it, and you are going to take it, and the difference between those two things is the only thing I have got left that is worth anything to anybody." He said it flatly and completely. "There are four years of quarterly folders in a cupboard in this house and I have read the first page of each one. I am going to read the rest of them, and I am going to tell you what is in them, and I am not doing it for you."

"For whom."

Mr Yeom looked at him.

"For the one who went out with no invoice," he said, "because he did not go out of a building. He went out of mine."

At the door, Georgij stopped, and it was Mr Yeom who spoke first.

"You will not come back either," he said. "Somebody has already told you not to, this month, and you agreed with her."

"A woman with a book in pencil."

"Then she is right and I am not going to improve on her." He had one hand on the frame. "But I am going to say a thing to you, and you are going to have to take it standing in a doorway, because you have taken everything else that way today."

"Then it can be said at the door."

"You were in this house in May and you had a rule and you kept it, and today you came back and broke it on purpose in front of a man who could do nothing for you." Mr Yeom did not look away. "I have been in this trade my whole life. I have never once seen anybody give away the thing that keeps them safe when there was no bill to pay with it."

Georgij stood in the doorway of a house in the suburbs and found he had nothing arranged.

"There was a bill," he said.

"Yes," said Mr Yeom. "I know. I only wanted to hear whether you would say so."

---

# Book Two · Chapter 54: Clause eleven
*Lot Fourteen* · Version 1.4 · EN

## Day Three Hundred and Seven · Thursday 6 August

He decided on the Wednesday night that he was not going to tell her first, and he wrote the reason down before he did it rather than afterward, because a reason written afterward is not a reason.

*Not because she would stop me. Because the moment I put it in front of her it becomes hers.*

*What I am about to build is the first thing this year that will exist on paper with her name nowhere on it.*

*I will tell her when it is done and before it is sent. That is the arrangement I am making with myself at half past eleven on a Wednesday, alone, and I am writing it here so that it is a promise and not an intention.*

The house on the river has been winding up since April.

There are no settlements. There is no desk and no glass panel and no chair on the visitor's side, and there is a man on the third floor with two crates and a schedule of things to be closed.

And it still keeps a permanent series.

That is the whole of what Georgij worked out on the Thursday morning, and it took him eleven weeks to arrive at, and it had been sitting in front of him the entire time.

A house that is winding up is still a house. Its terms of business bind it until somebody signs the series over to an archive or a successor, and until that morning it has to answer for what it holds. Nobody has told Georgij when that morning is.

Nobody has told Hwang either, because a fund decides that and a fund is in no hurry. It is the only reason this is possible in August, and there is no version in which it is still possible in the spring.

Mrs Sunwoo told him about the series in October, in a ballroom, without any idea what she was handing over. The new man tidied everything. One series, the whole thirty years in one sequence. Before him you could not find a lot from four years ago without knowing which of four systems it had been entered under, and now a girl of nineteen can find anything in the place in about a minute.

Georgij has thought of that as an obstacle for ten months. It is the reason the fourth line is a strike-through in a book that will outlive everybody, and a man who cannot be bribed cannot be gone round.

He sat at the desk in the small room on Thursday morning and turned it over for the first time.

A man who has built a system that cannot be gone round has built a system that cannot decline to answer.

The terms of business are eleven pages and Annie has a copy, because everybody who buys at that house signs a copy, and she has kept every piece of paper she has ever signed in a drawer that locks.

He asked Mrs Seo for the key at ten past nine and she gave it to him without asking why, which is a thing he thought about for the rest of the day.

It took him under a minute to find the file and he stopped with his hand on it.

October. Seven pages of conditions and a schedule at the back, and on the schedule, in a column, four figures and a lot number.

He has never read it.

He has known it existed since about the fourth day. He has walked past that drawer perhaps four hundred times. There has never been an hour in ten months in which he could not have opened it. He has told himself, when he thought about it at all, that there was nothing in it he did not already know.

He read it at the desk with the door open, because closing it would have made it a different act.

Most of it is a contract for the sale of a thing, and he had expected that, and it was still not the same as expecting it.

Clause four is about the condition of the item on delivery.

Clause six is about what the house will and will not warrant.

Clause nine is the one about the register, and the strike-through, and the fee, and it is three lines long and perfectly clear and it is why Byun had a price.

Clause eleven is about provenance.

*Where a bona fide interest is asserted in respect of any lot, the House shall upon written request supply a statement of record. The statement shall be prepared from the permanent series and shall be entered in the permanent series under the reference of the lot to which it relates. No statement shall be withheld on the ground that the record is nil.*

Georgij read that four times.

Then he sat back in a chair in a small room on the river and did the thing he does about once a year. He laughed at something that is not funny to anybody else and would not survive being explained.

The last sentence is the whole of it and it was written by a man who was proud of himself.

He put it into his own words on the page, because a sentence you have rewritten is a sentence you have understood.

*If somebody with a proper interest asks the house what it holds on a lot, the house has to answer in writing. The answer goes into the permanent series, under that lot, for ever. And the house is not allowed to stay silent just because the answer is nothing.*

*He wrote that clause so that nobody could ever again say the house had hidden a record. It also means the house cannot hide the absence of one.*

*A strike-through is a mark on a page and anybody can argue about what it means. A statement of record, prepared under clause eleven and entered in the permanent series, saying that as at a date in August the House holds no entry in respect of that lot, is a document. It is the house saying it, in its own series and its own hand, at a date after the sale. It cannot be taken out again, because the man who built the series built it so that nothing can.*

*That is not evidence of what happened to her. It is evidence that she was there and is not, and that is the thing nobody has been able to write down since the spring four years ago.*

The rest of Thursday was the hard part, and it was hard in the way that only writing is.

The request has to be from somebody with a bona fide interest, and it has to be about the right lot, and it has to be impossible to answer any way except the one way.

He drafted it eleven times.
